task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-14, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: play sequence (X -> Y within same possession)
methodological_questions: How to define temporal precedence within a possession?
What confounding factors affect PNR efficiency?
Is there sufficient sample size of sequences with teammate DRIVE then PNR?
How to isolate the effect of a preceding DRIVE from game context and defensive adjustments?
Are play-type labels reliable for identifying drives and PNRs?
Does labeling bias (foul leakage, context-dependent tagging) inflate or deflate sequential premiums?

historical_evidence.finding: Only 2/30 stars had a stable same top suppressor across seasons. Negative teammate pair: Giannis->Lillard DRIVE->PNR -0.263 (n=31).
Top teammate sequences: J. Brown->J. Tatum DRIVE->PNR +0.326 (n=43, later flagged as placebo artifact). D. Bane DRIVE->PNR -0.324 (n=70). Many cells DIRECTIONAL with n<50.
PNR share jumps +12.1pp playoffs vs RS possibly due to tagging differences; DRIVE allowed PPP drops -0.268.
Shot-level PNR share ranges 7.6–13.8% across teams; used for calibration of possession-level PNR labels.
Only 0.7% of possessions map to a play type via initiation_type. DRIVE PPP understated by 12pp due to foul leakage; OTHER PPP inflated by 36% foul endings.
Brown->Tatum DRIVE->PNR +0.326 later removed: 'doesn't hold up'. Sequence premiums abandoned for unknown reasons.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attempt to find stable teammate sequential suppressors (e.g., negative premiums) across seasons
failed_approaches.why: Only 7% of stars had a stable top suppressor; small sample per cell (min n=20).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Descriptive listing of teammate DRIVE->PNR premiums without multiplicity control
failed_approaches.why: Most cells directional with n<50; later shown a positive DRIVE->PNR premium was a placebo artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Assuming play-type PPP differences reflect true efficiency
failed_approaches.why: Labeling artifacts: DRIVE PPP understated due to foul leakage; only 0.7% mapping via initiation_type.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Sequential conditioning premium analysis including DRIVE->PNR
failed_approaches.why: Results abandoned; a specific positive DRIVE->PNR pair did not hold up (placebo artifact).

evidence_establishes: Teammate DRIVE->PNR sequence premiums have been observed but with mixed signs (both positive and negative), small sample sizes (n=30–70), and at least one previously reported positive premium (Brown->Tatum) was later identified as a placebo artifact.
Play-type labeling for DRIVE suffers from systematic foul leakage that depresses DRIVE PPP by approximately 12 percentage points.
PNR possession labels may shift across contexts (e.g., regular season vs playoffs) due to tagging inconsistencies.
The initiation_type mapping captures only 0.7% of possessions, indicating substantial labeling uncertainty.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether any true causal or robust sequential premium exists for a teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR.
Whether positive DRIVE->PNR premiums generalize beyond a few specific player pairs or survive correction for labeling artifacts and multiple testing.
Whether the labeled sequence 'DRIVE then PNR' corresponds to a clean, distinct tactical phenomenon or is contaminated by foul-drawing drives, defensive switches, or ambiguous possession tagging.
own_inferences: The combination of small cell sizes, labeling artifacts, and the documented placebo effect makes it very unlikely that a test of 'Any teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR raises PNR PPP' can attain useful statistical power with the current data.
Foul leakage on DRIVE labels could systematically bias the PPP of drives downward, which would inflate any apparent sequential premium if the subsequent PNR is not similarly affected.
Defensive adjustments after a drive (e.g., help rotations, switching) could confound the PNR efficiency in ways that are difficult to control for without granular tracking data.
uncertainties: Whether the calibrated PBPProxyPNR labels (referenced in [prior work][prior work]) would improve labeling reliability enough to rescue the analysis.
The exact criteria used to link a DRIVE and a subsequent PNR to the same possession and same teammate, and how robust those links are to clock and substitution mismatches.
Whether sufficient sample size exists when restricting to specific teammate pairs and game contexts to yield a precise estimate.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical evidence, one might assume that play-type labels are sufficiently reliable and that sequential premiums like DRIVE->PNR can be estimated directly from possession-level data. The fetched records reveal pervasive labeling artifacts (foul leakage, inconsistent PNR tagging), very small cell sizes for teammate sequences, and a documented placebo artifact for a previously reported positive DRIVE->PNR premium. These findings shift the assessment from 'testable with care' to 'likely not testable without major methodological changes and redesigned labels'.

blocking_constraints.text: Historical teammate DRIVE->PNR cells had n=30–70; many were labeled DIRECTIONAL. The question 'any teammate DRIVE' would pool all pairings, but to reach adequate power (>0.8) for a small effect in the presence of large game-level variance, a far larger number of sequences would be needed.

DRIVE PPP is systematically understated by ~12pp due to foul leakage (only 0.7% of possessions map via initiation_type). This bias can create or inflate apparent sequential premiums. PNR labeling may shift across contexts, further compromising the outcome variable.
A previously reported positive teammate DRIVE->PNR premium (Brown->Tatum) was later flagged as a placebo artifact. This raises the prior probability that any observed effect is spurious.
Testing 'any teammate DRIVE' implicitly involves many player-pair combinations. Unless a global aggregated test with appropriate shrinkage is prespecified, the probability of false positives is high.

prior_work.summary: Earlier work explored teammate sequential premiums including DRIVE->PNR and found mixed signs, small samples, and at least one artifact. The question has not been definitively answered because reported positive premiums were later discredited, and no study has tested the global hypothesis 'any teammate DRIVE raises PNR PPP' with corrected labels and rigorous controls.

risks.text: Systematic understatement of DRIVE PPP due to foul leakage; ambiguous possession tagging; 0.7% mapping rate may exclude most real sequences.

Pooled across all teammate pairs, the number of DRIVE->PNR sequences within the same possession may still be insufficient to detect a plausible effect size (e.g., +0.03 PPP) with power >0.8 given high possession-level variance.
Historical record shows at least one apparent positive DRIVE->PNR premium was a placebo artifact; the present test would need to rule out a similar artifact.
Defensive strategy (e.g., switching, help rotations) after a drive may affect the subsequent PNR, creating a spurious association if not controlled.
If the test is conducted pair-by-pair, the large number of teammate combinations inflates Type I error; if aggregated, the question 'any teammate' may be too vague and mask genuine heterogeneity.
Labeling distributions and team play-style change across seasons and between regular season and playoffs, potentially invalidating pooled estimates.

design.estimand: The difference in PNR points per possession when the PNR is immediately preceded by a teammate DRIVE (within the same offensive possession) versus when it is not, controlling for game score, period, defensive team, and possession start state.
design.unit: A PNR possession as recorded in the play-type possession graph, with the sequence DRIVE (by a different player on the same team) -> PNR within the same 24-second clock event.
design.sample: NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26 regular seasons (playoffs omitted due to documented PNR share drift). Only possessions where both the DRIVE and the subsequent PNR are labeled with high confidence (e.g., using a calibrated PBP proxy that corrects for foul leakage and mapping gaps).
design.power: For a minimum detectable effect of +0.03 PPP (roughly 0.1 standard deviations of possession-level PPP), with alpha=0.01 and power=0.9, approximately 5,000-7,000 DRIVE->PNR sequences would be needed. Historical evidence suggests only a few hundred exist even across all teams, so the test is underpowered.
design.controls: Fixed effects for offensive team, defensive team, period, score differential (binned), and possession start state (after made basket, defensive rebound, sideline out-of-bounds, etc.).
design.falsification: Test whether a subsequent PNR that is NOT preceded by a teammate DRIVE but is preceded by an equivalent 'non-action' (e.g., a dribble reset or an off-ball cut) yields a similar premium. Also test for placebo sequences where the DRIVE occurs after the PNR or in an unrelated possession.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a single global hypothesis: the weighted average of the conditional DRIVE->PNR premium across all teammate pairs (with shrinkage via hierarchical Bayesian model) is positive. No per-pair tests unless the global test is significant and then with FDR control.
design.decision_rule: Reject the null if the Bayesian posterior probability that the global premium > 0 exceeds 0.95, using a weakly informative prior centered at zero. Additionally, require that the effect withstands a leave-one-season-out cross-validation and is not driven by a single player pair.
design.data_version: Play-type possession records from [source] database as of 2026-06-14, augmented with the foul-leakage-corrected PBP proxy labels developed in SF-[prior work] and SF-[prior work] follow-up. Minimum 10 possessions per pair to be included in aggregation.
